======================================================================
Empirical Research Plan – Great Boston Fire of 1872
======================================================================

----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred design: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with an event-study extension.

Why DiD?  
• We observe the same spatial units (blocks / neighborhoods) repeatedly before and after an unexpected, spatially well-defined shock.  
• The fire line creates a sharp, plausibly exogenous distinction between “treated” (burned) and “untreated” (unburned) areas while broader Boston-wide shocks (railroad expansion, immigration waves, post-Civil-War boom) hit both groups.  
• With many pre-fire years we can test the parallel-trend assumption and estimate dynamic treatment effects (event study).  

Optional complement: a “border-DiD” that restricts the sample to blocks within, say, 500 m of the burn perimeter to tighten comparability, or an RDD in distance-to-fire-line for robustness.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment definition  
• treated_i = 1 if block i lies inside the official 1872 fire perimeter (burned)  
• treated_i = 0 otherwise  

Control group  
• Primary: blocks in Boston that are outside the burn perimeter but inside the 1870 municipal boundary.  
• Preferred “tight” control: blocks within a short radius (e.g., 500 m) outside the perimeter to ensure similar pre-fire land use and access to amenities.  

Timing  
• Event (t = 0) = 1872:Q4.  
• post_t = 1 for years ≥ 1873.  
• Lead/lag window: at least −20 ≤ k ≤ +40 years.  

No running variable is needed for the core DiD; distance to the perimeter will be used only in robustness checks.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Parallel pre-trends: in the absence of the fire, treated and control blocks would have followed the same growth path for property values, business counts, and population.  
 Plausibility: both areas were part of Boston’s core commercial district; pre-fire maps show similar land use. We can formally test this with pre-1872 coefficients in the event study.  

A2 No anticipation: actors could not foresee a specific catastrophic fire in 1872 far enough in advance to alter investment systematically.  
 Plausibility: fire was accidental; building patterns before 1872 show no discernible divestment.  

A3 Stable composition / SUTVA: the treatment status of one block does not directly affect the outcome of another block except through general-equilibrium channels that are common to both groups.  
 Plausibility: short-run spillovers (displaced firms) are possible; we will address by dropping immediate neighbors or using border-DiD.  

A4 Common measurement: property assessments and census counts are generated by the same city offices for all blocks.  
 Plausibility: high—city-wide tax assessment standards applied uniformly.  

----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Differential post-fire municipal policies (zoning, street widening) concentrated in burned areas.  
 Mitigation: control for post-fire block-level infrastructure investments (street width, sewer installation dates). Include interacted year-of-assessment fixed effects × “street-widened” indicator.

T2 Spatial spillovers—businesses displaced from burned blocks may temporarily boost activity in nearby controls (“negative contamination”).  
 Mitigation: exclude a buffer zone (e.g., first 100 m outside the fire line) or implement a triple-difference that compares near-perimeter vs. far-perimeter changes inside and outside the burn line.

T3 Reversion to the mean / differential long-run trends (e.g., waterfront vs. inland shifts).  
 Mitigation: (i) block fixed effects soak up time-invariant locational advantages, (ii) include block-specific linear or quadratic trends, (iii) use a matched-sample DiD based on 1870 characteristics.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast two-way FE
library(MatchIt)     # matching for robustness
library(broom)       # tidy output

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data (place CSV in working directory)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
fire_df <- read_csv("boston_fire_panel.csv")   # hypothetical file

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct key variables
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
fire_df <- fire_df %>%
  mutate(
    post          = as.integer(year >= 1873),
    treated       = as.integer(burned == 1),
    treat_post    = treated * post,
    # event_time: years relative to fire (1872 = 0)
    event_time    = year - 1872
  )

# Restrict to balanced panel if desired
fire_df <- fire_df %>% 
  group_by(block_id) %>% 
  filter(n() == length(unique(year))) %>% 
  ungroup()

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DiD Regression
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(log(prop_value) ~ treat_post +                 # coefficient of interest
                    i(year) + i(block_id) | 0,                   # two-way FE
                  data = fire_df, cluster = ~block_id)

summary(did_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event-study specification
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
es <- feols(log(prop_value) ~ i(event_time, treated, ref = -1) + 
              i(year) + i(block_id) | 0,
            data = fire_df, cluster = ~block_id)

iplot(es)  # dynamic graph of leads and lags

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: border sample (<=500 m from perimeter)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
fire_df_border <- fire_df %>% filter(abs(distance_to_perimeter) <= 500)

border_did <- feols(log(prop_value) ~ treat_post + i(year) + i(block_id) | 0,
                    data = fire_df_border, cluster = ~block_id)

summary(border_did)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. Robustness: matching on 1870 covariates
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
m.out <- matchit(treated ~ log(prop_value_1870) + pop_1870 + land_use,
                 data = fire_df %>% filter(year == 1870),
                 method = "nearest", ratio = 1)

matched_ids <- match.data(m.out)$block_id
fire_matched <- fire_df %>% filter(block_id %in% matched_ids)

match_did <- feols(log(prop_value) ~ treat_post + i(year) + i(block_id) | 0,
                   data = fire_matched, cluster = ~block_id)

summary(match_did)
```
Notes:  
• `log(prop_value)` is the primary outcome; parallel regressions will be run for `business_count` and `population`.  
• Replace `"boston_fire_panel.csv"` and variable names with actual file/column names.  
• `i(year)` and `i(block_id)` are short-hand for factor fixed effects in `fixest`.  
• Cluster at block level; clustering at neighborhood level can be a robustness check.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition suggests a J-curve:

Short-run (0–5 yrs): Severe decline. Property values in burned blocks may fall 30-50 % relative to controls due to destruction, insurance frictions, and temporary business displacement.

Medium-run (5–15 yrs): Rapid recovery as modern, fire-proof buildings are erected; municipal street-widening improves accessibility.

Long-run (15 + yrs): Net positive effect (+5–15 %) if new infrastructure, taller buildings, and agglomeration economies outweigh destruction costs.

Hence, I expect β_DiD ≈ −0.4 log-points (≈ −33 %) in 1873–1877, converging to 0 by ~1890 and turning positive thereafter.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
----------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel trends visible in pre-1872 data ………………… 0.8  
C2. No anticipation of treatment ………………………………… 1.0  
C3. Stable unit composition / no endogenous migration…… 0.6  
C4. No spillovers / SUTVA ……………………………………… 0.5  
C5. Consistent data measurement across groups …………… 0.9  

Overall: 3.8 / 5 – credible but not bullet-proof; requires careful pre-trend tests and spatial spillover checks.

======================================================================
